claims.text: Adding hBN to a refractory metal matrix will produce a self-lubricating composite.
An hBN-containing refractory metal matrix composite will preserve mechanical strength across a wide temperature range.
An hBN-containing refractory metal matrix composite will provide stable tribological performance across a wide temperature range.
Nickel or cobalt alloys are examples of the proposed refractory metal matrix.
Powder metallurgy can produce a uniform dispersion of hBN nanoparticles in the metal matrix.
The interfacial bonding of hBN particles to the matrix mediates the balance between load-bearing capacity and lubrication performance.
The dispersion quality of hBN particles mediates the balance between load-bearing capacity and lubrication performance.
At low temperatures, the metal matrix supplies the composite's mechanical strength.
At high temperatures, the layered structure of hBN facilitates shear between contacting surfaces.
Shear facilitated by hBN reduces friction.
Shear facilitated by hBN reduces wear.
Synergy between hBN and the metal matrix enhances tribological performance without compromising structural integrity.
Compared with the matrix-only baseline, the hBN composite will have a lower coefficient of friction from room temperature to 800 °C.
Compared with the matrix-only baseline, the hBN composite will have a lower wear rate from room temperature to 800 °C.
The hBN composite will retain adequate mechanical strength from room temperature to 800 °C.
A matrix composite without hBN may have greater mechanical strength than the hBN-containing composite.
A matrix composite without hBN lacks effective self-lubrication at elevated temperatures.
Excessive hBN content can embrittle the composite and diminish the strength-lubrication balance.
Operating above the thermal stability range of hBN can diminish the strength-lubrication balance, particularly under oxidizing conditions.
